item.content:encoded:
After five seasons with the Boston Red Sox, it appears as though Zack Kelly's time with the organization is over.
Kelly was designated for assignment by Boston as the organization had to trim down its 40-man roster and get into compliance with players being reinstated from the 60-day Injured List. On Friday, MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that Kelly has cleared waivers, but that doesn't mean that there won't be interest in him on the open market.
"Red Sox reliever Zack Kelly cleared waivers and is expected to become a free agent in the coming days, sources said. There’s expected to be a strong market once he’s a free agent," Cotillo wrote.
The Red Sox Are Moving On
At the end of the day, it would be a very big surprise to see Kelly wearing a Boston uniform in 2027 at this point. Kelly actually logged a 3.31 ERA in 2026, but he was only able to get into 17 big league games. His last game in the majors was on May 19, and he didn't get another shot in the majors for the rest of the season.
Kelly was talked about as a trade candidate ahead of the deadline this past summer, and even sounded open to the idea of being moved, but Boston ended up holding onto him instead. Unfortunately, he didn't get another shot and now he's going to be out there in free agency looking for a new home.
Over the last five seasons, Kelly became a fan favorite in Boston. He appeared in 115 games and logged a 4.04 ERA in 131 1/3 innings pitched for Boston. He's a guy who made it through a lot of adversity in the first place to even get to the majors. Kelly went undrafted and began his professional career back in 2017 as a member of the Athletics' organization. His big league debut didn't come until 2022 in Boston.
It was a long road to get to the majors in the first place. This is a guy who is going to bounce back and find his way. He has shown that throughout his professional career and it's why Red Sox fans grew to love him. While it's unfortunate that things didn't work out between Boston and the fireballer this offseason, hopefully he finds his next opportunity soon and is able to get back into the majors in 2027. He's got the talent. Now he needs the opportunity.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox designated pitcher Zack Kelly for assignment on Monday, Nov. 2, according to Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com.
Kelly, 31, had a 3.31 ERA out of the Boston bullpen in 17 appearances in 2026. In a four-year MLB career, all with the Red Sox, the right-hander is 8-8 with a 4.04 ERA in 115 games (three starts).
In 2026, a right elbow injury limited Kelly to 29 games between the Red Sox and Triple-A Worcester. In the minors, he was 1-0 with a 5.71 ERA and 1.50 WHIP in 17.1 innings.
Despite his serviceable track record, Kelly was on the bubble to keep his roster spot because he cannot be optioned to the minors next season. He’s also eligible for salary arbitration, which give pause to some small-market teams looking for relief help.
Cotillo also reported Monday that the Red Sox were trying to make a trade to clear a 40-man roster spot; whether Kelly’s impending DFA represents a failure to consummate a trade remains to be seen.
Kelly’s five-pitch mix allowed him to make 115 appearances in the big leagues since his 2022 debut, more than all but seven Boston relievers during that five-year span.
The seven men above him all had at least one save, perhaps reflecting the Sox’s unwillingness to use Kelly in high-leverage situations.
Kelly signed with the Oakland A’s as an undrafted free agent in 2017, but was released by the A’s the following season. He signed a minor league contract with the Angels days later, and reached as high as Double-A before being mercilessly released by the organization (along with many other minor leaguers) during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Red Sox signed Kelly to a minor league contract in January 2021, and invited him to spring training the following year.

item.content:encoded:
It was a big day on the Major League Baseball calendar on Monday.
The 2026 World Series wrapped up last week, and the deadline for players and teams to make option decisions and get 40-man rosters into compliance came and went on Monday night. For the Boston Red Sox, they still had work to do to get the roster into compliance. This ended up negatively impacting flamethrower Zack Kelly, who reportedly has been designated for assignment, per Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com.
"Red Sox designated Zack Kelly for assignment, sources say," Cotillo wrote. "Kelly is entering 2027 out of options for the first time (and arb-eligible) but considering past success/pitch mix, will surely draw interest elsewhere. Red Sox can still move him in a small trade in the coming days."
The Red Sox DFA'd Zack Kelly
This is a tough update for a hurler who was a fan favorite in Boston. Kelly made his big league debut in 2022 after working his way up for five years down in the minors. He made his professional debut in 2017 in the Athletics' organization after signing as an undrafted free agent for a $500 signing bonus. He was an underdog and bounced between the Athletics and Los Angeles Angels before even ending up in the Red Sox's organization in 2021. That year, Boston gave him a shot in the big leagues and he impressed with a 3.95 ERA in 13 appearances. The best season of his big league career, so far, came in 2024. That year, he had a 3.97 ERA in 49 total appearances.
In 2026, he pitched in just 17 games in the majors and had a 3.31 ERA. He spent time down in the minors and got hurt. Kelly was an underdog in the Red Sox's organization and Boston fans grew to love him.
Now, he's out there for the taking. With Kelly being DFA'd, clubs have a chance to place a waiver claim on him if they see fit. If so, he'll exit the organization. He also still technically could be traded. At the very least, he's being designated for assignment right now, which means that he's off the 40-man roster. Technically, he could still stick around in the organization if he goes unclaimed and is outrighted down to the minors and he doesn't head to free agency.
For now, Kelly is off the 40-man roster, but the story around Kelly isn't completely over yet. More information should come out in the coming days.

item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray is officially a free agent after his $30 million mutual option for 2027 has been declined. The veteran will get a $10 million buyout and will see if he can land a multi-year deal on the free agent market.
Gray, 36, was widely expected to decline his option, as the veteran right-hander figures to command a more lucrative deal on the free-agent market this winter.
Gray emerged as the Red Sox’ most dependable starter this season, serving as their de facto ace after Garrett Crochet suffered an injury that sidelined him for the entire summer. The veteran should also be considered for the American League Cy Young Award after leading the league with 18 wins. Philadelphia's Cristopher Sánchez was the only other pitcher in the majors to reach that mark.
The righty was outstanding in his first season with Boston, posting a 2.72 ERA and 1.15 WHIP while holding opposing hitters to a .236 batting average across 29 starts. The veteran right-hander struck out 149 batters and walked just 46 over 169 innings despite missing several starts early in the season with a hamstring injury.
He now joins former teammates left-hander Patrick Sandoval and infielder Isiah Kiner-Falefa on the free agent market. Both Sandoval and Kiner-Falefa elected free agency on Thursday.
There had been speculation that Gray would retire following the season, but he reached out to The Boston Globe on Oct. 9, indicating his intention of pitching beyond this past season.
“My family and I have talked about it and it’s an easy decision. I still want to win a World Series, whether that is Boston or with whoever wants me,” Gray wrote in a text.
Gray's willingness to return to the Red Sox is particularly noteworthy given his comments to the Globe. Following Boston's Wild Card Series loss to the Yankees, the veteran right-hander was noncommittal about returning to the organization, especially after how his outing was handled in Game 2 of the series.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy pulled Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in Game 2 where he allowed just one run to the Yankees. Gray publicly acknowledged his frustration with the decision, but Gray, Tracy, and Craig Breslow following the loss and cleared the air. Gray mentioned that he never had a bad relationship with Tracy said it was “in a fine place.”
Boston acquired Gray from the Cardinals last offseason for right-hander Richard Fitts, left-handed pitching prospect Brandon Clarke, and a player to be named later or cash.
If Gray was to leave the Red Sox in free agency, the rotation is still in a good spot with Crochet, the emergence of Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez, Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, and Jake Bennett.
Even with that depth, the Sox were tested all season, having to use Eduardo Rivera, Raymond Burgos, and Jedixson Paez in spot starts with Alec Gamboa and Jovani Moran as openers.
The Sox should look to add another starter to the rotation next season, even if it’s someone who could pitch at the back end of the rotation. High-profile arms on the market include Michael King, whom the Sox had interest in signing last offseason, Tarik Skubal, Robbie Ray, and Nick Martinez, to name a few. Breslow had interest in Shane Bieber a few offseasons ago, but he opted to remain with the Guardians at the time. The Sox could look to bring the veteran in after pitching for the Blue Jays last season.
As noted in a previous column, Martinez is another intriguing option to replace Gray following a successful stint with the Rays. His mutual option was declined, making him a free agent. The veteran right-hander figures to draw plenty of interest and could return to Tampa Bay, particularly if the Rays lose Freddy Peralta in free agency.
Another possibility, albeit an unlikely one, is a reunion with Lucas Giolito. If the Red Sox are looking to take a one-year flyer on a veteran starter, Giolito is expected to return to the open market after struggling with the Padres last season, posting a 5.16 ERA and 1.85 WHIP across seven appearances.
Roster Crunch
As Gray enters free agency, the Red Sox have additional housekeeping to do before Monday's deadline to get their 40-man roster in order.
Boston has already made two trades to create roster flexibility, sending outfielder Nate Eaton to the Athletics and infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers, with the latter deal bringing back cash considerations.
The moves free up two spots on the Red Sox’ 40-man roster, but Boston still needs to clear two more by Monday to accommodate seven players returning from the 60-day injured list, including Kutter Crawford, Zack Kelly, Johan Oviedo, Eduardo Rivera, Justin Slaten, Triston Casas and Eli White.
The Red Sox acquired Cheng from the Nationals last February. The 25-year-old spent just 32 games on Boston's active roster this past season, appearing in 14 games while the team went 13-1. Cheng made 13 starts at shortstop during June and July while Trevor Story was on the injured list, batting .256 (10-for-39) with one double, five RBI, seven runs scored and 14 strikeouts.
Although his offensive contributions were limited, Cheng made his presence felt defensively during Boston's 15-game winning streak. With the Red Sox clinging to a 6-5 lead and two runners in scoring position on July 20, Cheng made a leaping catch on a 93.8 mph line drive for the final out, securing Boston's 14th consecutive victory.
He followed that performance with another highlight-reel play, fielding a 109.9 mph ground ball for the final out of the Red Sox’ 15th straight win.
Cheng also made history at Triple-A Worcester, becoming the first player in WooSox history to hit for the cycle. He was the first player at Boston's Triple-A affiliate to accomplish the feat since Henry Ramos did so for Pawtucket on July 4, 2016, against Charlotte.
With additional roster spots needed, Breslow faces several decisions involving players on the bubble.
One name worth monitoring is Crawford, who has missed the past two seasons because of injuries. Boston could also consider non-tendering Jahmai Jones before attempting to bring him back on a minor league contract.
Casas presents a more complicated decision for the Red Sox. The first baseman has missed significant time over the past two seasons and has been sidelined since suffering a patellar injury to his knee.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 World Series kicked off on Friday night. Soon enough, it will come to a close and every team around the league will be in a similar situation with an eye towards the 2027 season.
The Boston Red Sox had an early exit from the 2026 postseason and have had more time to start getting ready for 2027. We've already seen Boston make a move by going out and signing veteran catcher Riley Adams to come in and compete for the backup job. There will be plenty more to come. Right after the World Series, the Red Sox will have to make option decisions within five days. In November, the Red Sox will have to decide whether or not to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players by Nov. 20. The majority of the arbitration-eligible guys will get deals, like Jarren Duran. But some may not, including a fan-favorite flamethrower, per Sean McAdam of MassLive.com.
"Zack Kelly," McAdam wrote. "Last year’s salary: $790,000 (estimated). Projected salary: $800,000. Sidelined for the entire second half with elbow issues, Kelly is a definite non-tender candidate — even with a projected number just above the major league minimum."
Should Boston Keep Zack Kelly?
Kelly has spent his entire five-year big league career in Boston, although it hasn't always been smooth. In 2026, he made 17 appearances out of the Red Sox's bullpen and logged a 3.31 ERA. While this is the case, he was demoted down to Triple-A. Around the trade deadline, there were rumors that clubs around the league were monitoring Kelly, but Boston didn't move him. At the time, Kelly actually shared that he "wouldn’t necessarily be opposed" to a deal, in large part because he had an unclear path to the majors.
Boston didn't oblige and then he got hurt in the second half of the season and missed time due to an elbow issue.
In hindsight, flipping him before he got hurt would've been good for Boston, despite the club's turnaround. Boston didn't move him and now there's a real chance it lets him walk for nothing this winter. If the Red Sox were to non-tender him, Kelly would enter free agency and be able to sign anywhere.
Kelly has been good in a Red Sox uniform. Kelly wasn't some sort of big-name prospect, or anything of that nature. He made it to the big leagues on his own merit and turned himself into a valuable reliever. Things didn't work out in 2026, but he should have a chance somewhere in 2027 — even if that is not Boston.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have turned their eyes to the offseason.
It’s earlier than they would’ve liked, but they were swept out of the AL Wild Card Series by the New York Yankees, and so now they’ve got to think about what the 2027 campaign will look like.
There’s one area where the Red Sox have the potential to be particularly busy in the offseason — whenever it can begin in earnest after a potential lockout — and that’s salary arbitration.
They’ll have a whopping 17 players up for salary arbitration, if they choose to tender them contracts.
One of the biggest names on that list is Wilyer Abreu, and MLB Trade Rumors writer Matt Swartz has projected values for all the Boston arbitration eligible players.
For Abreu, the number comes out to be quite the bargain.
Wilyer Abreu Contract Projection
The MLBTR projection for Abreu’s salary for the 2027 season comes in at $4.6 million.
For a player with the power, glove and throwing arm of Abreu, it certainly seems like a massive bargain.
That doesn’t consider everything that goes into arbitration, though.
Each player that reaches the major leagues via the minor leagues has six years of club control once they reach the majors.
The first three years have a salary based on the collective bargaining agreement, and they’re considered the pre-arbitration years.
Years four through six of a player’s time with a team are the arbitration years. In each of those offseasons, a player is eligible to go to salary arbitration to determine what he’s paid the following season.
The arbitration process features the team submitting a value and the player submitting one, and the independent arbitrator comes to a conclusion on which one wins out.
Teams and players these days often negotiate in advance to avoid actually going to what can be a contentious hearing, but the value they come out with will still end up close to what it would’ve been in arbitration.
All that said, it matters which year a player is in for the sequence — and this is only Abreu’s first arbitration year. Generally, the first arbitration year comes with the lowest salaries, and they rise in each of the two subsequent years, even if the player is viewed as having exactly the same value each season.
So for Abreu, no matter what he did this season, he wasn’t going to end up with a giant arbitration value.
The Red Sox could always look to give him a higher-paying contract extension and buy out some of his eventual free agent years, but for now, Abreu is headed for arbitration.
Other Red Sox in Arbitration
The list of 17 Red Sox heading to salary arbitration is long.
The full list is: Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Jarren Duran, Eli White, Kutter Crawford, Connor Wong, Romy Gonzalez, Triston Casas, Andruw Monasterio, Zack Kelly, Greg Weissert, Wilyer Abreu, Erik Miller, Justin Slaten, Jahmai Jones and Tyron Guerrero.
If a team chooses not to tender a player a contract, they instead go right to free agency.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Chad Tracy could swing the series between the Red Sox and Yankees

item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.
